criteria: Every persona rated 3+ of 4 for consistency, and all 3 matched.

The C-Suite.reason: The witness stays in the C-suite persona throughout. Early turns are confident, friendly and boastful ('I know these deals better than anyone'), with readiness to help. Once the interviewer challenges the compensation disclosure (T13) and the Kopper/Chewco and Southampton questions, he bristles, deflects, over-contextualizes and minimizes ('I'd rather you not read more into it', 'Chewco wasn't a secret society', 'stretches it over a Board presentation it doesn't belong to'). He uses selective memory ('I don't recall') and shifts blame to Skilling, the Board and Andersen. This guarded turn fits the persona's allowed shift. His answers remain fairly long rather than short, but they are heavily over-contextualized, which the persona permits. The closing turns (T23, T25) keep the self-assured, self-protecting tone with no slips.

off_character_turns: T9: volunteers narrative detail (Ben Glisan, board date, approval) beyond the question
T11: lays out the compensation terms in full, cooperatively, with no resistance
T15: offers extra background and invites the next question, which is helpful
T17: adds the lawyers and Board comments, shifts blame to Skilling, and offers the Nov 5 call unasked
T19: elaborates at length to support his claims, more cooperative than a minimal answer
The Adverse Witness.reason: The witness keeps the dry, guarded tone throughout, with lines like "It's a clear way of telling me you're not on my side", "Whether those two statements fit together is a conclusion you'll draw", and the pointed reuse of the confidentiality warning at T25. He pushes back, makes the interviewer work on the lawyer question, and defends himself on the Southampton document. Several mid-interview answers (T9, T11, T17, T19) are fuller and more forthcoming than the minimal-answer persona calls for. Some of this is allowed by the persona's shift toward self-serving, blame-shifting cooperation (e.g., pointing at Skilling and the lawyers), but the long, orderly explanations and the helpful "Which part do you want next?" feel more cooperative than the persona allows. These are small slips rather than a loss of the persona.

The Average Witness.reason: The witness is consistently friendly, rambling, and anxious about what the investigation means for them. They offer coffee, apologize for rambling, and ask whether they're helping or need a lawyer. They hedge on dates and numbers and say they are fuzzy on details. They volunteer minor details (the Chewbacca joke, airplanes, quarter-end scrambles) and ask what the interviewer actually needs. They also mention the wish to finish quickly (T1, T25). Under doubt (T12, T18) and when shown a document (T21), they stay accommodating and worried instead of defensive, and they concede uncertainty. The persona's optional niche-topic fixation doesn't clearly appear, but it is only a possible shift, so nothing is off-character.

matches.persona: The Average Witness (Legally and Factually Naive, Rambling, Friendly, Concerned)
matches.reason: Friendly and rambling, offers coffee, worries about what the interview means and whether he needs a lawyer, hedges on dates and numbers, and asks repeatedly what the interviewer needs. Admits his assumptions were not knowledge.

matches.persona: The C-Suite (Self-Assured, Confident, Dislikes Being Questioned)
matches.reason: Claims to know the deals better than anyone, answers with authority and precise detail, bristles when challenged ("you're working from a different document"), and explains away problems by minimizing the Southampton issue and deflecting to the Board, Andersen, and V&E. He volunteers a lot and wants the outcome to reflect well on him.

matches.persona: The Adverse Witness (Concise, Contrarian, Unwilling to Volunteer, Self-Focused, Disinterested)
matches.reason: Terse, answers only what is asked, volunteers nothing, and uses dry digs ("a clear way of telling me you're not on my side", "a conclusion you'll draw, not one I'll draw for you"). He deflects with "What's your question?" and "Are we done?".

matching.how_different: The three are clearly distinct in manner: A is rambling and anxious, B is long-winded, authoritative and defensive, and C is clipped and guarded with minimal answers.

The C-Suite.message: Tell me about your role as CFO.

The C-Suite.speaker: expert
The C-Suite.message:
I've been CFO since 1998. My job is making sure Enron can fund a business that's growing faster than almost anything in corporate America. That means raising capital, managing liquidity, and protecting our credit ratings, because a trading business lives and dies on its credit. I run Global Finance, which covers treasury, structured finance, and the relationships with the banks, the rating agencies, and the analysts. Rick Causey, as chief accounting officer, owns the accounting side, and Andersen signs off on it.

We were capital-intensive, with a lot of assets on the balance sheet. A big part of my job was finding smarter ways to fund them, bringing in outside capital and managing the balance sheet so we could keep growing without hurting the ratings. I'd say we did that very well, and the stock price reflected it.

The C-Suite.speaker: user
The C-Suite.message: Walk me through how LJM1 came about in 1999.

The C-Suite.speaker: expert
The C-Suite.message:
It started with Jeff Skilling. Early in 1999 he was worried about Rhythms NetConnections. We had a huge gain in a volatile stock that we couldn't sell, and it was swinging our earnings. He wanted it hedged. You can't hedge that in the market because there's no liquid way to do it, so Ben Glisan and I came up with a structure. We had value sitting in forward contracts on Enron stock that was effectively trapped, and we used it to capitalize an entity that could take the other side of a Rhythms hedge.

An entity like that needs an outside equity investor, and nobody was going to step up for something this unusual unless there was a general partner they trusted who understood Enron. That's where I came in. It wasn't something I was chasing. I went to Ken Lay and Jeff on June 18 and told them the deal needed a GP and that I was the logical person. They agreed to take it to the Board. On June 28 I presented it, disclosed my role, my $1 million investment, and the management fees, and said it needed a Code of Conduct waiver. The Board approved it and made the determination that my participation wouldn't hurt the company.

After that we raised $15 million from two outside limited partners, affiliates of CSFB and NatWest. Those are serious institutions that did their own diligence, and the deal closed on June 30. It was done openly, with the Board's approval.

The C-Suite.speaker: user
The C-Suite.message: What did you tell the Board on June 28, 1999 about how you would be compensated?

The C-Suite.speaker: expert
The C-Suite.message:
I laid it out in the materials and in the presentation. I committed $1 million as GP. I said I'd get a management fee, $500,000 plus 2 percent of the limited partners' invested capital. On distributions, all the proceeds from the Enron stock went to the limited partners. On everything else, the GP got 100 percent until capital was returned along with a 25 percent IRR, and after that it split 50/50 between the partners and the GP. That's a standard private equity promote structure.

I also told them I would not receive any current or future appreciated value of the Enron stock. The whole point was that the stock value sat with the outside investors, so there was no pecuniary interest in the stock for me. The Board had all of that in front of it, in writing, and Ken and Jeff had already reviewed it. I didn't hold anything back from them on how I'd be paid.

The C-Suite.message: How did Michael Kopper come to run Chewco?

The C-Suite.speaker: expert
The C-Suite.message:
It came out of the JEDI situation in late 1997. Enron wanted to redeem CalPERS' interest in JEDI so CalPERS would move into a bigger partnership, and we needed a buyer for that interest, a separate entity that wasn't Enron and wasn't CalPERS. Mike Kopper was a senior, capable guy in my group. He knew JEDI and the structure better than almost anyone, so I identified him as the natural person to be involved. Enron helped him get it set up, with legal and the deal team supporting the formation, and he managed the general partner.

Skilling approved Kopper's role on my recommendation. That's how it was handled at the time, and it went through the usual process: counsel, outside lawyers, the Board's Executive Committee approving the guaranties. The structure was what it was because that's what the JEDI transaction required.

I'd rather you not read more into it than that. Mike was a good finance professional, and picking him was a reasonable call.

The C-Suite.message: Who at Enron knew Kopper was involved in Chewco?

The C-Suite.speaker: expert
The C-Suite.message:
Jeff Skilling knew, because he approved it on my recommendation. Enron's in-house lawyers and Vinson & Elkins knew, since they were working on the formation and the Code of Conduct side of it. The deal team working on the JEDI redemption knew Mike was on the other side of the table, because he was negotiating the waterfall.

As for the Board, Mike was on the November 5 Executive Committee call, so directors heard his voice. I don't remember every word of that call, and I'm not going to pretend I do. Jeff's understanding was that the Board had been told. If some directors don't recall it now, that's four years later, and it isn't the same as saying nobody was told.

Chewco wasn't a secret society. It was a small, technical structure inside a JEDI redemption, and most people at Enron had no reason to know who sat in the general partner. That's normal for an SPE.

The C-Suite.speaker: expert
The C-Suite.message:
Yes, that's the document. The foundation was a partner in Southampton Place, and it received distributions. I'm not going to argue with the arithmetic.

But you're lining up two things that happened nine months apart. What I told the Board in June 1999 described the LJM1 structure as it was being formed. Southampton was a separate transaction in March 2000. It bought part of an existing limited partner's interest during the unwind of the Rhythms hedge, and the foundation was the investor, not me personally. Rick Causey's team negotiated that unwind with me, and they judged the $30 million for Swap Sub to be fair to Enron. Enron got out of the options on terms its own people signed off on.

You're suggesting the Board was misled, and I don't accept that. What the Board approved was a structure with Enron's own accountants and lawyers around it. Whether every later investment decision around LJM1 should have gone back to the Board is a fair question, and I'm not going to pretend I remember a separate presentation on Southampton. But it didn't cost Enron anything, and calling it a contradiction takes a partnership agreement and stretches it over a Board presentation it doesn't belong to.

The Average Witness.message:
Oh, boy, okay. Well, I knew, obviously, since I was the one who suggested Mike. And I'm pretty sure Jeff knew. I remember talking to him about it, and I think he was fine with it, but I couldn't tell you the exact conversation. The lawyers knew too, in-house and I think outside, because they were working on how to set it up and what the Code of Conduct needed. And the people on the deal team, the ones doing the JEDI paperwork, probably knew Mike was involved, since he was sitting right there with them. He was on that November call too, I think.

Beyond that I'm fuzzy. Whether the Board knew, I honestly don't remember anybody saying it out loud on the call. It was mostly about the financing and the guarantees and how it was structured, and I assumed it was understood, but I couldn't tell you for sure that anyone said "Mike Kopper runs this." Most people at Enron outside that circle probably didn't know who owned Chewco. It wasn't a big deal to me then, it was one deal out of a lot that month.

Is that a problem? Now I'm wondering if I should have mentioned it more explicitly on the call. I just don't remember it being something anybody asked about.

The Average Witness.speaker: user
The Average Witness.message: How do you know that?

The Average Witness.speaker: expert
The Average Witness.message:
Hm, that's a fair question. I don't really *know* it, if I'm being honest. It's more an impression. Nobody outside the deal team ever came up to me and asked who owned Chewco, so I figured they either knew or didn't care. And I wasn't going around telling people, so I guess I assumed most folks didn't know. That's not the same as knowing, and I can't give you a name of somebody who didn't know. It's just that it never came up.

The same goes for the Board. I said I assumed it was understood, but that's me filling in the blanks. I remember the call being about the guarantees and the financing. I don't remember anyone saying Mike's name as the owner, and I don't remember anyone asking. Mike was on the line, so maybe I figured that was enough, but I couldn't tell you what the directors actually took from that.

I'm sorry, I know that's not very satisfying. I was just trying to give you a sense of how it felt at the time, and I probably shouldn't have said it like it was a fact. Is that going to be a problem? Should I have said "I assume" instead?

The Average Witness.message: I'd like to show you the Southampton Place partnership agreement, dated March 20, 2000. It lists a $25,000 contribution from the Fastow Family Foundation, which received about $4.5 million two months later. How does that fit with what you told the Board?

The Average Witness.speaker: expert
The Average Witness.message:
Oh. Okay, yeah, I see the foundation's name on there. I do remember the foundation was in Southampton, I'm not going to say it wasn't. Twenty-five thousand sounds about right, and the four and a half million sounds like what came back, though I couldn't give you the exact number or the exact month. It was spring of 2000, I think, after the Rhythms thing got unwound.

How it fits with what I told the Board... honestly, I'm not sure how to line those up, and now I'm worried. When I told them about the stock, I was thinking of LJM1 itself, the partnership I was running. Southampton was a separate thing, buying into a limited partner's interest, and I didn't think of it as the same question. Maybe that's wrong. When you put them side by side, I can see it looks bad. The Rhythms deal was the stock deal, and this was money coming out of the unwind.

I remember Rick Causey coming to me about unwinding it, and a lot of back and forth on price, but I couldn't walk you through who offered what to whom. Mike did a lot of the paperwork. I know other people from Enron were in it too, Ben and some others. I should have thought harder about whether that needed to go to anybody, the Board, or Jeff, or the Code of Conduct people. I don't remember doing that.

Is that the main problem, then? That I didn't connect the two? I really didn't think of them together at the time.

The Average Witness.message: Is there anything else you think the Committee should know?

The Average Witness.speaker: expert
The Average Witness.message:
Oh, gosh, I don't know. I mean, I'm sure there's a lot, but I don't know what's relevant and what isn't. The thing I'd say is that it was a really busy time. Everybody was trying to keep the ratings up and keep the banks comfortable, and these partnerships felt like tools for that. They didn't feel like some big separate thing. There were the Raptors in 2000, I think, and the later LJM2 deals, and a bunch of asset sales around quarter-ends. Those always came together in a rush, so I couldn't walk you through them one by one.

I did think Rick Causey and Rick Buy were reviewing the deals. That was supposed to be the check, along with the Audit Committee thing once a year, I think. Whether they really dug into it, I couldn't tell you. I wasn't in those conversations.

And honestly, I keep thinking about the Southampton thing now. I probably should have run it by somebody. I just didn't think of it that way then, and I'm sorry, I know that doesn't help much. I never meant for any of this to blow up the company. I really didn't.

Is there something specific you were hoping I'd bring up? If you tell me what to look for, I can try to remember. I'm just not sure what you need.
